Patterns in FONSIs: Deliverable 6

Categorical-exclusion opportunities from prior clean-energy Findings of No Significant Impact

Published

June 25, 2026

Executive Summary

Key Findings
  • Every bounded, low-impact clean-energy action has a text-similar existing CE candidate (pending verification). None looks net-new (0 to develop), and none exceeds a parsed limit in its matched CE candidate (no deterministic expand candidates under the current heuristic). The likely opportunity is to adopt / harmonize an existing CE — 4 candidate adopt opportunities, pending CE-coverage adjudication.
  • The clearest case is transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way: 37 bounded, low-impact FONSIs across BLM, DOE, and the power-marketing administrations, for work TVA already covers under its CE #17.
  • Most clean-energy FONSIs lean on committed mitigation — 310 of 452 (69%) are mitigated FONSIs, so a CE built from them must encode the recurring mitigations as design criteria, not rely on case-by-case commitments.
  • Adopting a peer agency’s CE is well-precedented: of 2,105 existing federal CEs, 130 action-families are already shared across two or more agencies.
  • Net-new CEs most likely lie outside this candidate set — in the ~159 clean-energy FONSIs not yet categorized (the recommended next step).

This report delivers:

Technical support for new regulatory categorical exclusion development: identifying patterns in FONSIs.

Under CEQ’s April 2026 CE guidance, a prior Environmental Assessment that ended in a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) is explicit, citable substantiation for a CE — so recurring clean-energy FONSIs are the natural evidence base for new, expanded, or adopted categorical exclusions.

Method note. Action definitions, numeric limits (acreage, line length, voltage, well count), and the mitigation read now come from a one-pass LLM enrichment of all 451 clean-energy FONSIs (Claude Sonnet), with every quoted value verified verbatim against its cited source page (97% verified). The CE-coverage match remains a ranking aid pending eCFR confirmation.

Methodology

The deliverable runs three analyses, each on a different data source. They are not a single funnel — only Analysis 1 starts from the full FONSI corpus; Analysis 2 works from the mitigated subset of it, and Analysis 3 works from the existing federal CE catalog (not FONSIs at all).

Analysis Data source Scope
1 · Scaling CEs (develop, expand, or adopt) Decarb EAs with FONSIs 53/452 projects (~12%)
2 · Mitigated FONSIs Decarb Mitigated FONSIs 310 of 452 projects (69%)
3 · Current federal CE catalog Existing federal CE catalog 2,105 CEs
Steps for each analysis

Analysis 1 · Scaling CEs

  1. Data — the 452 clean-energy EA→FONSI projects. A FONSI concludes a full Environmental Assessment, so each is a documented federal “no significant impact” determination — the evidence base for a CE.
  2. Sort each FONSI into a candidate action type (transmission upgrades, solar, geothermal exploration) by keyword and technology.
  3. Keep the bounded, low-impact subset within each type — the small, routine projects that could plausibly be a CE (in-corridor upgrades, not major rebuilds).
  4. Match each candidate against the existing federal CE catalog by text similarity.
  5. Read the matched CE’s stated size limits (acres, miles, kV, MW, wells), where it has any.
  6. Classify as develop (no existing CE covers it), expand (our FONSIs exceed the CE’s stated limit), or adopt (a CE exists, but at a different agency than the ones doing these FONSIs).

Analysis 2 · Mitigated FONSIs

  1. Data — the mitigated FONSIs: the subset whose “no significant impact” finding depends on committed mitigation rather than the action being inherently low-impact (310 of 452, 69%).
  2. Flag each FONSI’s mitigation dependence from the LLM read — case-specific-dependent (the finding rests on committed mitigation) vs design-feature-only (inherently bounded) vs none.
  3. Measure the mitigated share and the resource areas where mitigation recurs, within each action type.
  4. Read for CE design — a mitigation that recurs consistently across a class is a codifiable CE design criterion; an idiosyncratic one is a disqualifier.

Analysis 3 · Current federal CE catalog

  1. Data — the existing federal CE catalog (the CE Explorer export — 2,105 CEs across 78 agency units, each linking to its eCFR source).
  2. Compare every CE to every other by text similarity.
  3. Flag near-duplicates that recur at more than one agency.
  4. Group those into shared “action families.”
  5. Read each CE’s stated numeric limits, where it has any → what is already covered and how routinely agencies share the same CE (the precedent for adopt).

Analysis 1 — Scaling CEs (develop, expand, adopt)

Every bounded, low-impact clean-energy action already has a text-similar existing CE at another agency. None looks net-new (0 to develop) and none exceeds a stated CE limit (0 to expand) — so all 4 resolve to adopt: agencies are running full EAs on actions a peer agency already categorically excludes (pending eCFR confirmation of each match).

The four candidates, and what “adopt” means

  • Transmission upgrades → adopt the Tennessee Valley Authority’s CE for routine modification, repair, and minor upgrade of existing transmission (CE #17), so BLM, DOE, NNSA, and the power-marketing administrations can stop running full EAs for in-corridor work.
  • Solar (CE-shaped subset) → adopt the Department of Energy’s small-solar CE for bounded projects on previously disturbed land.
  • Geothermal exploration → adopt the Department of Energy’s exploration-drilling CE for slim-hole / temperature-gradient wells.
  • Temporary resource assessment → adopt the Department of Energy’s site-characterization CE for surveys, stream gauges, and geotechnical borings.

The outcome at a glance

Steps 1–2 · Sorting the FONSIs into action types

Each clean-energy FONSI is sorted into a candidate action type, and within each type we keep only the bounded, low-impact subset (teal) — the small, routine projects that could plausibly be a CE — and set the rest aside. The 159 uncategorized FONSIs are the net-new search pool (Analysis 3).

Step 3 · Matching to the existing CE catalog

Each candidate is matched against the federal CE catalog by text similarity. The score blends embedding (semantic) and lexical overlap; below 0.40 we would treat the action as needing a new CE. Every candidate clears the bar — the match is a ranking aid, confirmed against the CE’s eCFR text before action.

Step 3 · The size bounds a CE could encode

For each candidate we read the size figures the bounded FONSIs actually state — the observed range is the candidate numeric bound a CE could codify. None of the matched CEs state a limit our FONSIs exceed, so nothing resolves to expand; but the spreads below are what a newly written or adopted CE would set its thresholds against.

Step 4 · Classifying and ranking the candidates

Each candidate gets a transparent multi-factor rank score (0–1) built from how novel it is (develop > expand > adopt), how many FONSIs support it, its agency/state spread, whether it has size limits, and how mitigation-dependent it is. The bar length is the total; the colors show each factor’s contribution.

The transmission case is the most geographically broad — the same in-corridor work runs through full EAs across 12 states, concentrated in the West.

Timing · do these EAs predate the FRA?

The 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act (FRA, June 2023) gave agencies explicit authority to adopt another agency’s categorical exclusion — the exact move this analysis recommends. So the age of these EAs matters: every dated FONSI in the bounded set was decided before the FRA, meaning these agencies ran full EAs without the adoption shortcut now available. (Decision dates are only partially populated in the current data; a merge with the D4 timeline would firm up coverage.)

Worked example: transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way

The strongest-evidenced case: 37 bounded, low-impact FONSIs for in-corridor transmission upgrades (reconductoring, component replacement, minor rebuilds), across BLM, DOE, NNSA, and the power-marketing administrations in 12 states. The Tennessee Valley Authority already holds a CE for this class of work — TVA CE #17, “Routine modification, repair, and maintenance of, and minor upgrade of and addition to, existing transmission infrastructure…”

Analysis 2 — Mitigated-FONSI analysis

A FONSI can mean two different things: the action is inherently low-impact, or it reaches “no significant impact” only because the applicant committed to mitigation. That distinction is central to CE development — a CE cannot lean on case-by-case mitigation, so if an action’s FONSIs are routinely mitigated, a defensible CE for it must bake those recurring mitigations in as design criteria.

Mitigated-FONSI share

The shares are high — 89% of transmission-upgrade and most geothermal-exploration FONSIs depend on committed mitigation. This is the LLM’s per-FONSI mitigation_dependence read, and the result is striking: of the 310 mitigated FONSIs corpus-wide, 309 are case-specific-dependent — the no-significant-impact finding rests on project-specific mitigation, not on the action being inherently low-impact. That is precisely the CE-design challenge: a CE cannot lean on case-by-case commitments, so a defensible CE for these actions must encode the recurring measures (below) as standing design criteria.

A high mitigated share is double-edged: it is a risk (the action is not unconditionally benign) but also an opportunity — when the same mitigations recur across the class (here, consistently water, biological, and cultural resources), they become the natural, codifiable conditions of a CE. Transmission and geothermal are the clearest: a strong, recurring mitigation profile an adopted CE could formalize.

Boundary language (preliminary)

Alongside mitigation, the enrichment pass captures the agency’s explicit significance-threshold statements — “would be significant if it exceeded X,” “an EIS would be required unless Y.” Those sentences are a CE’s natural numeric bounds. Each is a verbatim, span-verified quote (with metric/value/unit parsed where stated), so the candidate bounds are now citable rather than directional.

Analysis 3 — Current-CE analysis

To know whether an action is “develop,” “expand,” or “adopt,” we first mapped the entire existing federal CE body: 2,105 categorical exclusions across 78 agency units, embedded and compared to one another.

Numeric bounds in existing CEs

Only 86 of 2,105 CEs state a numeric limit (acres, miles, kV, MW); the rest are qualitative. So an “expand the stated limit” argument has few existing precedents to lean on — part of why nothing resolved to expand in Analysis 1.

Cross-agency duplication

317 CEs are near-identical to a CE at a different agency, forming 130 action-families shared across two or more agencies. Adopting a peer agency’s CE is not unusual — it is how the existing landscape already works.

The largest shared families are administrative (procurement, personnel, routine maintenance) — which is the point: when an action is genuinely low-impact, agencies converge on the same CE. The clean-energy actions in Section 1 are simply ones where that convergence hasn’t happened yet.

Where net-new CEs would come from

Net-new CEs are empty here by construction: the candidate action types we hand-picked are all well-trodden, so all are already CE’d. But of the 452 clean-energy FONSIs, only 293 fell into those types — the remaining ~159 are other clean-energy actions we have not yet categorized. Net-new CEs most likely live there. The recommended next step is to cluster those un-categorized FONSI action descriptions to surface recurring categories nobody has hand-picked.

Caveats & next steps

  • LLM-extracted, verified facts. Action definitions, numeric limits, mitigation dependence, and significance thresholds come from a one-pass enrichment of all 451 clean-energy FONSIs (Claude Sonnet); every quoted value was checked verbatim against its cited source page (97% verified). Values that did not verify are flagged, not shown.
  • CE matches are a ranking aid, not verified coverage. Confirm each candidate CE against its eCFR text before acting on it — this is the one remaining verification step.
  • Recommended next steps: (1) verify the 4 adopt matches against the eCFR CE text; (2) cluster the ~159 un-categorized clean-energy FONSIs to search for net-new CEs.

For CATF: tell us which adopt opportunities to pursue, and whether to launch the net-new search — and we fold your direction into the next iteration.

Reproduction

Run from the repository root in the nepa conda environment:

conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable06/_run.py
quarto render phase2/reports/deliverable06.qmd

_run.py executes the numbered chain 01→08 (the 08_analyze.R figures step needs Rscript). Outputs are written to:

  • phase2/data/analysis/deliverable06/ — analysis parquets (verdicts, mitigation, CE landscape/clusters)
  • phase2/output/deliverable06/ — figures/, the slim comparison table, and review/ drill-down tables
